numerical_check_note: Lesson-generated numerical values were independently recomputed: 5.0 × 0.80 = 4.0 m s⁻¹ and 12 × 0.25 = 3.0 m s⁻¹. Reverse division checks reproduce the stated frequencies.

hints: For each type, compare particle displacement with the direction of energy transfer.
Use the words perpendicular and parallel in the appropriate places.
walkthrough: Identify the two directions used for classification: particle displacement and energy transfer.
A transverse wave is a wave in which the displacement of particles is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
A longitudinal wave is a wave in which particle displacement is parallel to the direction of energy propagation.
State both controlled definitions exactly.

ai_rubric.observable: States that a transverse wave is a wave in which the displacement of particles is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
States that a longitudinal wave is a wave in which particle displacement is parallel to the direction of energy propagation.

evidence.evidence_gap: This is a deliberate direct retrieval of verified Lesson 4 learning rather than a new Lesson 5 evidence demand.

hints: Recall the relationship joining wave speed, frequency and wavelength.
The units are already hertz and metres.
walkthrough: The known values are f = 5.0 Hz and λ = 0.80 m.
Use v = fλ.
Substitute: v = 5.0 s⁻¹ × 0.80 m = 4.0 m s⁻¹.
Therefore select option B. A reverse check gives 4.0/0.80 = 5.0 Hz.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects B, corresponding to 4.0 m s⁻¹.

hints: Compare vertical particle motion with horizontal energy transfer.
walkthrough: Particle displacement is vertical and energy transfer is horizontal.
Vertical and horizontal directions are perpendicular.
Perpendicular particle displacement defines a transverse wave.
Option A states both the correct type and reason.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects A, identifying perpendicular particle displacement as transverse.

hints: Sound in air is longitudinal.
Think about the direction of local air-particle oscillation, not travel from source to listener.
walkthrough: In a longitudinal wave, particle displacement is parallel to energy propagation.
Sound energy travels through the air toward the listener.
Air particles oscillate locally along that same line and do not travel all the way to the listener.
Therefore option C is correct.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects C, stating that air particles oscillate parallel to energy transfer.

hints: Compare up-down motion with left-right energy transfer.
walkthrough: The painted point moves vertically.
Energy is transferred horizontally along the rope.
Vertical and horizontal directions are perpendicular.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the painted point's displacement is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.

hints: Use the perpendicular relationship found in part (a).
walkthrough: Part (a) establishes perpendicular particle displacement and energy transfer.
That relationship is the defining test for a transverse wave.
Classify the rope wave as transverse.

ai_rubric.observable: Classifies the rope wave as transverse.

hints: Separate the motion of one piece of rope from the motion of the disturbance.
Recall what a progressive wave transfers.
walkthrough: The painted point is one piece of the rope medium.
It oscillates locally up and down about equilibrium.
The pulse or disturbance advances along the rope and transfers energy.
There is no net transport of the painted piece from one end to the other.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the painted point oscillates locally about its equilibrium position.
Distinguishes travelling energy or disturbance from net transport of the rope material.

evidence.evidence_gap: The mapped evidence directly supports particle direction and local oscillation. Compression and rarefaction identification is required by the canonical lesson specification.

hints: Look for a region where coils are closer than normal.
walkthrough: At P the spring coils are closer together than their normal spacing.
A crowded region in a longitudinal wave is called a compression.
Therefore P is a compression.

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies P as a compression.

hints: Look for a region where coils are farther apart than normal.
walkthrough: At Q the coils are farther apart than their normal spacing.
A spread-out region in a longitudinal wave is called a rarefaction.
Therefore Q is a rarefaction.

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies Q as a rarefaction.

hints: A longitudinal wave has particle displacement parallel to propagation.
walkthrough: The wave travels horizontally along the spring.
For a longitudinal wave, coil displacement is parallel to wave travel.
The coil therefore oscillates left and right along the spring.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the coil oscillates horizontally along the spring, parallel to wave travel.

hints: Track one coil rather than the crowded pattern.
Explain how a new crowded region forms farther along the spring.
walkthrough: One coil moves back and forth only near its equilibrium position.
It does not travel along the spring with the compression.
Its motion affects neighbouring coils, which then move closer together.
The crowded pattern therefore propagates as successive neighbouring coils become compressed and then spread again.

ai_rubric.observable: States that individual coils oscillate locally rather than travelling with the compression.
Explains that the compression propagates as neighbouring coils successively become closer together.

evidence.evidence_gap: The mixed wave-equation stage deliberately exercises verified earlier-module learning.

hints: Twelve complete pulses each second gives the frequency.
Use the spacing between successive identical pattern points as the wavelength.
walkthrough: The known values are f = 12 Hz and λ = 0.25 m.
Use v = fλ.
Substitute with units: v = 12 s⁻¹ × 0.25 m.
This gives v = 3.0 m s⁻¹. A reverse check gives 3.0/0.25 = 12 Hz.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses v = fλ with f = 12 Hz and λ = 0.25 m.
Obtains 3.0 m s⁻¹.

hints: Compare vertical particle displacement with horizontal energy transfer.
walkthrough: The marked rope point oscillates vertically.
The wave energy travels horizontally.
These directions are perpendicular, which identifies a transverse wave.

ai_rubric.observable: Classifies the rope wave as transverse.

hints: Name both physical directions before stating their relationship.
walkthrough: Read the particle direction: the marked point is displaced vertically.
Read the energy direction: the pattern transfers energy horizontally to the right.
Vertical and horizontal are perpendicular.
That perpendicular relationship justifies the transverse classification.

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies vertical particle displacement and horizontal energy transfer.
States that the particle-displacement and energy-transfer directions are perpendicular.

evidence.evidence_gap: Boundary-check item derived from the lesson's direction-based classification model.

hints: Ask whether the definitions of the two wave types contain a speed value or a direction relationship.
walkthrough: Wave speed tells how quickly the pattern propagates.
Both transverse and longitudinal waves can have many different speeds.
Wave type instead depends on how particle displacement is oriented relative to energy transfer.
Therefore speed alone cannot determine the wave type.

ai_rubric.observable: States that wave speed alone cannot determine wave type because classification depends on directions.

later_knowledge_excluded: Detailed displacement graph interpretation is reserved for Lesson 6.
Wave intensity is reserved for Lesson 7.
Polarisation and later Waves topics are excluded.
